From P.L. Deane, BRIGHTON

Dear Ron,

Has anybody been able to convert
the TASDIARY program from micro-
drive to Opus Discovery disc? If
not, does anyone know of a simi-
lar type of program?

I have just acquired an Epson
PX8 Laptop and, having now man-
aged to get it working, I am
wondering if it is possible to
run it together with my Spectrum
Plus with the Opus disc drive.
Can anybody help me?

         Thanking you,

          P.L. Deane


Brian Cavers to P.L. Deane


If TASDIARY uses machine code
hook codes then to access the
microdrives then it will not be
easy to convert to Opus disc.

I assume the Epson PX8 laptop is
a laptop PC computer - not a lap
top printer?

If it is a printer it should
just plug in the Opus Centronics
port and switch to Epson mode
(if necessary).

If it is a PC computer then it
is not clear HOW you want it to
work with your Spectrum. What do
you want to do exactly?


One of the most common diffi-
culties with readers problems is
not giving enough information so
I have to resort to guessing!...

Do you want the Epson to use the
Opus disc drive? - Almost no way
while still in use by a Spectrum
and difficult to rewire even if
you strip it down although some
expert enthusiast might get it
to work.

Do you want the Spectrum to use
the Epson disc drive(assuming it
has one - possibly it only has
RAM drives?). Again, very nearly
impossible.

Do you want to share a printer?
Yes, with a printer switch you
can do that.

Do you want to pass programs
from one machine to the other?
Almost impossible directly as
they are totally incompatible.It
should be possible to convert a
BASIC listing if compatible.

Do you want to pass text files
from one to the other? This may
have been possible if the Opus
had an RS232 port but as it is
there is no realistic way by
direct cable connection. If the
Epson has a 3.5" drive it may be
possible with the right software
to read text off an Opus disc in
the Epson and vice versa. Does
anyone know?
                     - Brian

From: Dave Newell, READING



Dear OUTLET,

In response to your request for
information about ink jet
printers, perhaps you might find
the following information
useful...

I bought a Kodak Diconix 150+
portable printer secondhand (2
months old) for `140.00 in
December, 1991. As far as
features are concerned, I've
enclosed a review that appeared
in MicroMart at about the same
time (which is how I discovered
OUTLET).


Information not mentioned is the
cost of refills which I buy for
about `11.50 each and thses last
for quite some time considering
they're smaller than your thumb!


If my memory serves me correctly
I've used three since I bought
the printer and, to be honest,
I'm a sucker for printing out
graphics which are quite demand-
ing in terms of ink consumption.
Kodak say that you will get a
minimum life of 10 million dots
from a cartridge - work that one
out!

Quality of printed output
depends very much on the type of
paper used.


There are also two types of ink
cartridges available: one for
plain paper use, the other for
ink jet paper. The ink jet paper
seems to give the best quality
but tends to be quite expensive.

You don't say whether or not you
want the printer for graphics or
text but bear in mind the
graphics resolution isn't done
any justice when it's hooked on
to a Spectrum. You cannot down-
load fonts to this particular
printer but Kodak have intro-
duced more recent(and expensive)
models with fonts built in.


The graphics resolution figures
are as follows...


Mode:      Normal      Expanded
           ------      --------

Single
Density  80x96 dpi   60x192 dpi


Double
Density  160x96 dpi  120x192 dpi


Double
Speed,
Double
Density  160x96 dpi  120x192 dpi


Quad

A sample graphics printout is
enclosed. The text demo is built
into the printer itself and one
thing worth mentioning is that
ouput can be as slow as 29 cps
average - based on 100 lines of
full width text, when printing
in Quality mode (as this letter
is).

I hope this is of use to you.

          Dave Newell

Brian Cavers to Dave Newell

Yes, of great interest. I was
disappointed in the printing
speed but realize that you are
describing a compact portable
and full-size ink jet printers
would be faster.

I'm not sure what to make of the
claim to get 10 million dots for
`11.50! If you take a page of A4
with say text 9" deep by 7" high
at quadruple density of 320 x 96
dots per inch I calculate that
to be...
         10000000/(320*96*7*9)

              ...a mere 5 pages!

Shurely shome mishtake?
                         - Brian

From Alan D. Cox, ST. CLEARS


Dear Brian,

I seem to recall that some while
ago, the question was raised
whether VAL$ was of any real use
-I have not checked back for the
reference in earlier editions
since OUTDEX does not help with
letters.

Now you may well aruge that I
was in any case trying to do
things in a daft way - I would
not argue with such a view - but
I recently came across a situa-
tion where VAL$ did exctly what
I wanted: alternatives were not
obvious.


Background: I wanted to explore
the distribution of the digits
in the expression for PI. I have
got about 40,000 digits but only
either on a Macintosh disk or
else in hard copy and of course
I cannot read a Macintosh disk
(I have put out a plea within my
local compputer club for someone
who can translate Macintosh-
formatted disks to SAMDOS or
MSDOS format).

Since I did not want to wait for
a possible translation, I
decided that I would feed the
first 1000 or so digits in by
hand from the hard copy, so I
included in a program a PROC
that was a set of lines: LET
a$="..." LET b$="..." etc.


In order to do a simple check
that all the strings were of the
correct length (the hard copy
gives them in blocks of 72, so I
used this for my LET statements)
I then wanted to calculate their
lengths. So, tried...

   PRINT LEN (CHR$97+n)+"$")

               ...for various n.
Of course, this gives the value
2 for all n,since it is actually
giving the length of e.g., the
string "a$" - not the length of
the string a$. The solution...

PRINT LEN VAL$ (CHR$ 97+n)+"$")

          Alan D. Cox

Brian Cavers to Alan Cox

YES! This certainly looks like a
genuinely useful application of
VAL$! It also suggests other
applications, the main principle
being that a normal string (as
distinct from an array) can be
"calculated" in a similar way to
calculating the element of an
array but with the advantage the
individual strings can vary in
length. It can be used without
the LEN bit directly on the
string itself for instance to
print a sequence of strings...

FOR N=65 TO 70
PRINT VAL$ (CHR$ N+"$")
NEXT N
           ...to print A$ to F$.


Some BASICs on other computers
dimension string arrays in a
different way to Sinclair with
each element being of any length
and not fixed by the DIM.This is
useful at times, especially to
save memory or to save special
PRINT routines where the excess
spaces need to be dropped.A kind
of "pseudo" random length array
might be thus utilised on the
Spectrum where the calculation
to PRINT or process each string
would use VAL$(CHR$ N+"$")rather
than the usual A$(N) etc. It is
a pity there is no apparent way
to define the strings other than
one by one though! One would
probably use a calculated GO SUB
to INPUT A$, B$, C$ etc in turn.

                     - Brian

From Brian Birkett, DURHAM

Dear Brian,

As requested, please find some-
what bulky printouts of the
varying suggestions you made.
[following page overspill on a
24-pin printer using TABLOID]
I hope I am not being a burden.
(well just a teeny bit I hear
you say!)

To explain:- my Panasonic
KX-P1124 (24 pin) printer in
question initialises at 11" form
length along with basic font
parameters, but Skip perforation
and Auto linefeed are not set
and can be controlled under
software control (see photo).


Instead of DIP switches, all
parameters are controlled by the
touch sensitive keypad on the
front outside panel.

I have included a copy of the
set-up pages from the manual but
even if I set the form length to
11" at the operator panel, I
still get the same effect as
mentioned in my letter.

I demonstrate with OUTLETTERS
using TABLOID, numbering
printouts from 1 thro'4 to ease
identification:-


1) printout I described using
settings as on power up of
printer.


2) the result of modification to
LINE 1610 as you suggested, the
printer being re-initialised by
switching off, then after a few
seconds switching back on again.

3) reverting LINE 1610 to normal
with printer re-initialised and
set for sheet feed. It can be
seen from the printout this has
an effect,though not the desired
one. Note: the printer did not
pause at all until reaching the
end of the whole printout for
trial 3 & 4. also, I do not have
the sheet feeder option KX-P36
installed (please see photo page
3-13 Item(10)) although settings
for paper feed and roller dir-
ection are available supposedly
to allow hand feeding.


4) using sheet feed and adding
mods to LINE 1610 (E$;"CE";)
gives yet another combination as
can be seen from the result.
I trust this makes some sense to
you, because to me it just comp-
ounds the situation.

To get away from my problems I
have always needed to have an
index but as yet I simply have
not got around to completing the
assembly of all the data into
OUTDEX. I have not all issues of
OUTLET and naturally am inter-
ested in rectifying this but I
need to know which issues to buy
first. This is governed by the
contents. The availability of
such an index would serve to
promote and generate sales of
previous OUTLETS.

Since you must have an index
from which you work and OUTDEX
is up to capacity, and you are
considering the next move,
OUTDEX could be a stand alone
volume to date. Have you ever
thought of selling copies of it,
after all, most of the hard work
must be done already?

Since you made no mention about
my second 3.5" disk connection
query, (my letter Outlet 67 - in
reference to letter from Steven
are awaiting feedback. I am not
sure of the power connection on
the Spectrum +2 board so the
project is on hold.

May I enter the 'Centrifugal
Force' debate re: OUTLET 66,
F.G.MILES?

Centripetal force (centre seek-
ing force) is the constant force
necessary to maintain circular
motion.


The centripetal force 'F' acting
on a body of mass 'm' is given
by the equation F=m*v*v/r, where
'v' is velocity and 'r' is
radius of its path.


The centripetal force:the action
is balanced by a reaction force,
the centrifugal (centre fleeing)
force, which acts not on the
circling object but on the
source of the centripetal force,
usually located at the circle's
centre.


The solution is I think to be
found in the fact there are two
forces in play, equal in magni-
tude and opposite in direction.

This missing force,not mentioned
by name before, which balances
out the centrifugal (centre
fleeing) force,is called Centri-
petal (center seeking) force.

If a spring balance is placed in
the centre of the string to
measure the force involved, is
it [the measured force] the
encircling objects centrifugal
effort or that of the centri-
petal reactionary force, or
simply the tension force in the
string as a result of both
forces?


Laws of Physics dictate that
centripetal force acts as a
tension force in the string thus
balancing the Centrifugal force.
This is all fine but:-

If the string were to break at
some point along the weight's
orbital path, the weight would
follow a straight line at a
tangent from its release point.

But what of the effect on the
central anchorage point, say a
stone pillar, if the orbiting
weight was heavy enough, a stone
pillar would be liable to coll-
apse as a result but can this be
attributed to a Centripetal
force transferring its energy
along the string and pushing the
pillar over?

Brian Cavers to Brian Birkett

Thanks for all the info.

The characters in your 24-pin
print-out are .5mm higher than
the standard 8-pin text. I was
quite surprised and can't help
wondering if this is standard
for 24-pin printers. If so, it
would seem anyone with a 24-pin
printer would have this problem
but we don't seem inundated with
readers reporting this fault.

It might be worth checking your
printer manual to see if there
is any way of reducing height of
text but I doubt it. It was not
apparent in the photocopied
section you sent.


However,I think I have an answer
although it may make the print
look a bit squashed!

BREAK into the BASIC and add a
new line...

1607 POKE 64817,18

This will reduce the line space
BETWEEN the text. I have had to
guess at the 18 so if it is not
quite right try adjusting it up
or down slightly. The value
represents 216ths of an inch
from the top of one line of text
to the top of the next and the
original default was 24.

I am hopeful that once it fits a
sheet the form feed will be O.K.


I am sorry but I seemed to have
overlooked your disc drive query
but the answer is yes, connect
to the +2 cassette +5 and GND.It
should not be necessary to dis-
connect the tape deck but it is
recommended that you do not use
the cassette recorder while the
drive is in operation as the
extra voltage drain may cause an
error. For example, if you press
PLAY by accident while saving a
file on disc it is possible that
it may corrupt the disc. It may
be worth adding a switch to the
cassette connection and keeping
it OFF unless you need to use
tape.Do you think it likely that
you may accidentally press a key
on the tape deck while using the
drive?


I have now almost completed some
enhancements to MASTERFILE and
am modifying the instructions so
will publish this in a future
issue of OUTLET. I also found it
was not too difficult to write a
little BASIC routine to read all
the data out of the original
OUTDEX into a MASTERFILE file so
this will all be published soon.
It was interesting to find the
capacity was about the same! I
got only one more issue's data
into MASTERFILE than OUTDEX! It
is much faster and more flexible
than OUTDEX though so well worth
while and a second volume of the
OUTDEX will begin monthly from
when MASTERFILE is published. If
you need more detail,ask for our
BACK ISSUES list with brief des-
criptions of items.

You must have missed some of the
input on the centrifugal force
controversy as the term "centri-
petal" was raised some time ago
as being the correct term for
the (only) force involved.

I don't honestly follow your
description except to say it
makes sense to me that there are
TWO forces involved (as I said
all along!). You sound like you
are quoting so I'll take your
word for it but it seems to me
that the centripetal force (the
centre-seeking force) is the
"pulling" or "attracting" force,
e.g., the gravity or string in
our previous discussions, not
the "action" as you say. Indeed,
you go on to say the centripetal
force IS at the centre.

I've never tried pushing string
but I have wondered what force I
exert with my head when I bang
it against the wall. I wouldn't
mind but the wall always seems
to exert an equal and opposite
force which is a real pain.

                         - Brian.

From: Charlie Kingwell, OAKHAM

Dear Ron,

As I haven't written to you for

Brian Cavers to Charlie Kingwell

Yes, you HAVE missed something!
There IS an underline facility
in OUTWRITE described in the
manual under the printer codes.
You just use Menu 1, X, U to
insert an inverse capital "U" in
the text. Any text after this
will be printed out underlined.
Use a small "u" to switch it off
again.

After examining the fonts you
sent us it is clear they are two
sets of characters sets joined
together. I cannot believe that
Carol Brooksbank would sell them
like this without explanation so
look back at her instructions!
They must be intended for some
special purpose.

They can easily be split by just
loading them and resaving them
in two parts, each 768 bytes
long. Since they are on +D disc
you can load them directly into
your SAM Coupe and split them.
Just use something like...

LOAD "NAME"CODE 32768
SAVE "NAMEa"CODE 32768,768
SAVE "NAMEb"CODE 32768+768,768

You could save them to tape and
reload into your Opus using a
false header or SAMBYTES (OUTLET
39) but I took pity and did it
for you on your Opus disc!

They can be loaded straight into
OUTWRITE using FONTLOAD(Menu 2).
I am assuming you have Version 2
of OUTWRITE!           - Brian.

PRINT LEN (CHR$97+n)+"$")
